questions.question: Contoso's Azure Backup vault has soft delete enabled with the default retention. A ransomware attacker deletes a backup item, then the team discovers the deletion the next day. A colleague says the backup is gone. What actually happens, and how long does the team have?
options: Soft delete retains the deleted backup item for 14 days by default (extendable to 180 days), during which it can be restored; the team has that window to recover it
Soft delete retains the item for 30 days only, and it cannot be extended
Soft delete only works for VMs, not for other backup items
The backup is deleted immediately, because soft delete only protects the vault, not items
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Azure Backup soft delete retains a deleted backup item for 14 days by default, extendable up to 180 days, during which the item can be recovered; the retention is configurable and the always-on option exists. D is wrong: soft delete protects deleted backup items. B is wrong: the default is 14 days and it is extendable to 180 days. C is wrong: soft delete applies across backup item types, not only VMs.

questions.question: Contoso wants to ensure that even a compromised vault administrator cannot delete backups or disable soft delete. A colleague proposes soft delete alone. What is the stronger control, and why?
options: Soft delete alone, because it cannot be disabled by anyone
Immutability (locked) on the vault, which is irreversible and prevents deletion or modification of backup data even by a vault administrator; soft delete alone can be disabled by an administrator
A longer soft delete retention, because that is the same as immutability
Cross-region restore, because it prevents deletion
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Locked immutability on a Recovery Services vault is irreversible: once locked, backup data cannot be deleted or modified, even by a vault administrator. Soft delete alone is weaker because an administrator can disable it. A is wrong: soft delete can be disabled. C is wrong: longer retention is not immutability. D is wrong: cross-region restore is a recovery capability, not a deletion prevention control.

questions.question: Contoso enables multi-user authorization (MUA) with a Resource Guard for its backup vault. A vault administrator (who also holds Contributor on the Resource Guard) tries to approve a critical operation themselves. What happens, and why?
options: The operation is approved, because MUA only applies to deletions, not to other critical operations
The operation is blocked, because Resource Guards cannot be used with backup vaults
The operation is approved, because the vault administrator can approve their own requests

The operation is blocked, because the vault administrator must not hold Contributor, Backup MUA Admin, or Backup MUA Operator on the Resource Guard; MUA requires a different owner to approve critical operations
questions.explanation: Correct: D. MUA with a Resource Guard requires separation of duties: the person approving a critical operation must be a different owner from the requester, and the vault administrator must not hold Contributor, Backup MUA Admin, or Backup MUA Operator on the Resource Guard, because those roles would let them approve their own request. C is wrong: self-approval defeats MUA. A is wrong: MUA covers critical operations broadly, not only deletions. B is wrong: Resource Guards are the MUA mechanism for backup vaults.
questions.source_title: Multiuser Authorization Using Resource Guard - Azure Backup
questions.source_quote: "A different user must own the Resource Guard instance. The backup admin must not have Contributor, Backup MUA Admin, or Backup MUA Operator permissions for Resource Guard in any scenario."

questions.question: Contoso's primary Azure region suffers an outage. The team needs to restore a VM from backup in the secondary region. A colleague says cross-region restore works automatically for any vault. What is the correct prerequisite?
options: Cross-region restore requires locally-redundant storage, because GRS blocks restores
Cross-region restore requires the vault to be in the secondary region already
Cross-region restore works automatically for any vault, with no prerequisites
Cross-region restore requires the vault to use geo-redundant storage (GRS), because the backup data must be replicated to the paired secondary region before it can be restored there
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Cross-region restore requires geo-redundant storage (GRS): the backup data is replicated to the paired secondary region, and only then can it be restored there. C is wrong: CRR is not automatic; GRS is the prerequisite. A is wrong: LRS keeps data in one region and cannot support CRR. B is wrong: the vault stays in the primary region; the data is replicated to the secondary.

questions.question: Contoso restores a VM from a backup in the secondary region using cross-region restore. The team expects the restored VM to be in the primary region. Where does the restored VM actually land, and what is the implication?
options: In the secondary region, because cross-region restore restores into the paired secondary region; the team must plan for the workload to run there (or fail back) after the restore
In a third region of the team's choice, because CRR lets the team pick any region
The restore fails, because CRR cannot restore VMs
In the primary region, because restores always return to the primary region
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Cross-region restore restores the workload into the paired secondary region; the team must plan for the workload to operate from the secondary region (and fail back later if needed). D is wrong: CRR does not restore to the primary region. B is wrong: the secondary region is the paired region, not an arbitrary choice. C is wrong: CRR can restore VMs.

questions.question: Contoso's backup vault uses geo-redundant storage. A colleague says GRS keeps 3 copies of the data in one region. What does GRS actually provide, and why does it matter for backup?
options: 3 copies in one region, because GRS is the same as LRS
6 copies across 2 paired regions (3 in the primary, 3 in the secondary), so backup data survives a regional outage and supports cross-region restore
1 copy in each of 6 regions, because GRS replicates globally
2 copies in the primary region only, because the secondary is just a metadata copy
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Geo-redundant storage keeps 6 copies across 2 paired regions (3 synchronous copies in the primary region and 3 in the paired secondary region), which is why it survives a regional outage and enables cross-region restore. A is wrong: 3 copies in one region is LRS. C is wrong: GRS replicates to one paired secondary region, not 6 regions. D is wrong: the secondary holds full data copies, not just metadata.

questions.question: Contoso backs up an AKS cluster using the Operational Tier (snapshots) only. A ransomware attacker deletes the snapshots. A colleague says soft delete will recover them. What is the correct understanding?
options: Operational Tier snapshots are not protected by soft delete; the team needs the Vault Tier (with soft delete and immutability) for ransomware-resilient AKS backups, and cross-region restore for a regional outage
Operational Tier snapshots are protected by immutability automatically
AKS backups cannot use the Vault Tier, so the team must accept the risk
Soft delete will recover the snapshots, because it protects all backup tiers
questions.explanation: Correct: A. AKS Operational Tier backups are snapshots that are not protected by soft delete; ransomware-resilient AKS backup requires the Vault Tier (which supports soft delete and immutability), and cross-region restore for regional resilience. D is wrong: soft delete does not protect Operational Tier snapshots. B is wrong: immutability is not automatic on the Operational Tier. C is wrong: AKS backups can use the Vault Tier.
questions.source_title: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) backup support matrix - Azure Backup
questions.source_quote: "For backups stored in the Operational Tier, the underlying snapshots aren't protected by soft delete and can be permanently deleted."

questions.question: Contoso wants to restore an AKS cluster to a different region after a regional outage. A colleague says Operational Tier snapshots can be restored cross-region. What is the correct approach?
options: Restore the Operational Tier snapshots cross-region, because snapshots are region-independent
Use the Vault Tier with cross-region restore, because Operational Tier snapshots are region-bound; the Vault Tier replicates backup data to the secondary region for cross-region AKS restore
Recreate the cluster manually, because AKS backups cannot be restored cross-region
Use soft delete, because soft delete enables cross-region restore
questions.explanation: Correct: B. AKS cross-region restore requires the Vault Tier with cross-region restore enabled; Operational Tier snapshots are tied to the source region and cannot be restored cross-region. A is wrong: snapshots are region-bound. C is wrong: Vault Tier CRR supports AKS cross-region restore. D is wrong: soft delete is a deletion-protection control, not a cross-region mechanism.

questions.question: Contoso's backup vault is in a resource group that an attacker compromises. The attacker tries to delete the vault itself. A colleague says deleting the vault deletes the backups, and nothing can prevent it. What protects the backups?
options: Geo-redundant storage prevents vault deletion
Nothing can prevent vault deletion, so the backups are lost

Soft delete and immutability protect the backup data, and MUA with a Resource Guard can require a separate approval for critical operations including vault deletion, so a compromised vault admin alone cannot destroy the backups
Cross-region restore prevents vault deletion
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Vault deletion is a critical operation that MUA with a Resource Guard can gate behind a separate approver, and immutability (locked) prevents deletion of the backup data itself; together they stop a compromised vault administrator from destroying backups. B is wrong: these controls exist for exactly this scenario. D is wrong: CRR is a recovery capability, not a deletion control. A is wrong: GRS replicates data; it does not block vault deletion.

questions.question: Contoso's team deletes a backup item and then immediately tries to restore it, but the restore fails. A colleague says soft delete only works after 24 hours. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Soft delete retains the deleted item, but the restore must target the soft-deleted item (not the original item name) and the item must still be within the soft delete retention window; a restore attempted against the live item (rather than the soft-deleted copy) will fail
Soft delete does not apply to backup items, only to vaults
The item was deleted with MUA approval, so it cannot be restored
Soft delete only works after 24 hours, so the team must wait
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A soft-deleted backup item is recoverable within its retention window, but the restore must be performed against the soft-deleted item; attempting to restore the original (now deleted) item as if it were still live will fail. D is wrong: there is no 24-hour delay before soft delete applies. B is wrong: soft delete protects backup items. C is wrong: MUA approval does not make a soft-deleted item unrecoverable.

questions.question: Contoso wants to test its backup restore procedure without affecting production. A colleague proposes restoring to production and deleting the restored VM afterwards. What is the better approach?
options: Test by deleting a production VM and restoring it, because that is the only realistic test
Restore to production and delete the restored VM afterwards, because that is the only way to test a restore
Restore to an isolated test resource group or virtual network (a restore drill), so the procedure is validated without touching production resources
Skip testing, because Azure Backup restores always work
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Restore drills should target an isolated test resource group or virtual network, validating the restore procedure without risking production. B is wrong: restoring to production for a test risks the live environment. D is wrong: restores must be tested; assuming they work is how outages become disasters. A is wrong: deleting production to test a restore is reckless.

questions.question: Contoso's backup policy runs daily, but the team discovers that a critical database was not backed up for a week because the backup job failed silently. A colleague says Azure Backup has no alerting. What should the team configure?
options: Azure Backup alerts and monitoring (backup alerts, Azure Monitor integration, and Log Analytics) so failed jobs surface as alerts instead of failing silently
A longer retention, because retention fixes failed jobs
Cross-region restore, because it fixes failed jobs
Nothing, because Azure Backup has no alerting
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Azure Backup integrates with Azure Monitor and provides backup alerts (including job failure alerts) so a failed backup surfaces instead of failing silently; the team should configure alerts and monitor backup health. D is wrong: alerting exists. B is wrong: retention governs how long backups are kept; it does not fix failed jobs. C is wrong: CRR is a recovery capability, not a monitoring fix.

questions.question: Contoso uses Azure Backup for VMs. A colleague proposes also using Azure Site Recovery for the same VMs, saying the two are the same. What is the difference, and when is each appropriate?
options: They are the same, so the team should use only one

Azure Backup provides point-in-time backup and restore of data, while Azure Site Recovery provides disaster recovery (replication and failover of whole workloads to another region); Backup is for data recovery, Site Recovery is for business continuity after a regional outage
Azure Backup is for disaster recovery and Site Recovery is for data backup, so the colleague has them backwards but they are interchangeable
Azure Backup only works for on-premises VMs, while Site Recovery only works for Azure VMs
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Azure Backup is point-in-time backup and restore (recover data, files, or VMs to a point in time), while Azure Site Recovery replicates workloads and fails them over to another region for disaster recovery; they are complementary, not interchangeable. A is wrong: they serve different purposes. C reverses them. D is wrong: both work for Azure VMs (and Backup also covers on-premises via MARS).

questions.question: Contoso's backup vault soft delete retention is set to 14 days. A backup item is deleted on day 1, and the team tries to recover it on day 20. A colleague says it can still be recovered because the vault is immutable. What is the correct outcome?
options: It cannot be recovered, because soft delete only works for 7 days
It can be recovered, because immutability extends soft delete retention

It cannot be recovered: the soft delete retention window is 14 days, so after day 14 the item is permanently deleted; immutability prevents deletion of live backup data, it does not extend the soft delete window for an already-deleted item
It can be recovered, because soft delete is always 180 days regardless of the setting
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Soft delete retention is a fixed window (14 days by default, extendable to 180 days); once it expires, the deleted item is permanently removed. Immutability protects live backup data from deletion; it does not resurrect an item whose soft delete window has expired. B is wrong: immutability does not extend the window. D is wrong: 180 days is the maximum, not the default. A is wrong: the default is 14 days, not 7.

questions.question: Contoso wants to back up an Azure file share so that individual files can be restored to a point in time. A colleague says Azure Backup can only restore whole shares. What is the correct capability?
options: Azure Backup for Azure Files supports item-level (file-level) restore, so individual files can be restored to a point in time without restoring the whole share
Azure Backup cannot back up file shares at all
Item-level restore requires cross-region restore to be enabled
Azure Backup can only restore whole file shares, so the team must restore the entire share
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Azure Backup for Azure Files supports item-level restore: individual files can be recovered from a backup snapshot without restoring the entire share. D is wrong: item-level restore exists. B is wrong: Azure Files is a supported backup workload. C is wrong: item-level restore does not require CRR.

questions.question: Contoso backs up VMs in a Recovery Services vault with locally-redundant storage. A regional outage makes the primary region unavailable. A colleague says the backups can be restored in the secondary region because LRS replicates. What is the correct understanding?
options: LRS keeps 6 copies across 2 regions, so the backups are available
LRS automatically converts to GRS during an outage
LRS replicates to the secondary region, so the backups can be restored there
LRS keeps data in the primary region only, so the backups are unavailable during a regional outage; cross-region restore requires geo-redundant storage
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Locally-redundant storage keeps copies within the primary region only; it does not replicate to a secondary region, so a regional outage makes those backups unavailable and cross-region restore is impossible. GRS (6 copies across 2 paired regions) is required for regional resilience. C and A describe GRS, not LRS. B is wrong: storage redundancy does not change automatically during an outage.

questions.question: Contoso's backup vault uses zone-redundant storage (ZRS). A colleague says ZRS protects against a regional outage. What does ZRS actually protect against?
options: A regional outage, because ZRS replicates across regions
A zonal outage within the region: ZRS replicates data across availability zones in the same region, so it survives a zone failure but not a full regional outage
A single disk failure only, because ZRS does not replicate at all
A vault deletion, because ZRS blocks deletion
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Zone-redundant storage replicates data across availability zones within the same region, so it survives the loss of a zone but not a full regional outage; only GRS (paired secondary region) covers a regional outage. A is wrong: cross-region replication is GRS. C is wrong: ZRS does replicate across zones. D is wrong: ZRS does not block deletion; immutability and MUA do.

questions.question: Contoso enables cross-region restore on a vault that already has backups. A colleague says the existing backups are immediately available in the secondary region. What is the correct expectation?
options: Existing backups are never available cross-region; only new backups are
CRR is instant because GRS replicates synchronously
Existing backups are immediately available in the secondary region

Cross-region restore requires the backup data to be replicated to the secondary region, which takes time; Learn notes that items can take up to 48 hours to appear in the secondary region after CRR is enabled
questions.explanation: Correct: D. After CRR is enabled, backup data must replicate to the paired secondary region, and items can take up to 48 hours to appear there; existing backups are not instantly available cross-region. C is wrong: replication takes time. A is wrong: existing backups do become available after replication. B is wrong: GRS replication to the secondary region is asynchronous, not synchronous.

questions.question: Contoso wants to move a Recovery Services vault from locally-redundant to geo-redundant storage to enable cross-region restore. A colleague says the storage type can be changed at any time. What is the correct constraint?
options: The storage type is fixed at vault creation and can never be changed under any circumstances
The storage type can be changed at any time, with no restrictions

The vault's storage redundancy can only be changed before any backup items are protected in the vault; once backups exist, the redundancy type is locked (or requires the vault to be recreated / items removed)
The storage type can be changed, but only from GRS to LRS, never the other way
questions.explanation: Correct: C. A Recovery Services vault's storage redundancy can only be changed while the vault has no protected items; once backup items exist, the redundancy type cannot be changed in place, so the team must plan the redundancy (and CRR) before the first backup. B is wrong: the change is restricted once items exist. D is wrong: the restriction is not directional. A is wrong: it can be changed before any items are protected.

questions.question: Contoso backs up a SQL Server running on an Azure VM. A colleague proposes using the MARS agent on the VM, and another proposes the Azure VM backup extension. Which is correct for SQL on an Azure VM, and why?
options: The MARS agent, because it is the only way to back up SQL on an Azure VM

The Azure VM backup (with the SQL workload-aware extension), which provides application-consistent backup of SQL Server on Azure VMs; the MARS agent is for on-premises machines and file/folder backup, not for Azure VM workload backup
Neither, because SQL on Azure VMs cannot be backed up
Both are required together, because neither works alone
questions.explanation: Correct: B. SQL Server on an Azure VM is backed up through Azure VM backup with workload-aware protection, giving application-consistent SQL backups; the MARS (Microsoft Azure Recovery Services) agent is for on-premises servers and file/folder backup to Azure. A is wrong: MARS is not the Azure VM path. C is wrong: SQL on Azure VMs is a supported backup workload. D is wrong: only the VM backup path is needed.

questions.question: Contoso's team wants to back up files from an on-premises file server to Azure, with no VM backup involved. A colleague says Azure Backup cannot protect on-premises machines. What is the correct mechanism?
options: Cross-region restore, which backs up on-premises servers
Azure Backup cannot protect on-premises machines, so the team must use a third-party tool
The Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) agent, installed on the on-premises server, which backs up files and folders (and system state) to a Recovery Services vault
The Azure VM backup extension, which can be installed on on-premises servers
questions.explanation: Correct: C. The MARS agent protects on-premises machines by backing up files, folders and system state to a Recovery Services vault; it is the on-premises file backup path. B is wrong: on-premises backup is supported. D is wrong: the VM backup extension is for Azure VMs. A is wrong: CRR is a restore capability, not a backup agent.

questions.question: Contoso enables immutability on a vault and then tries to disable it during a cleanup, but the option is greyed out. A colleague says this is a portal bug. What is the correct explanation?
options: Immutability can only be disabled after 180 days
It is a portal bug, because immutability can always be toggled off

Locked immutability is irreversible by design: once locked, it cannot be disabled, which is what makes it a ransomware defence; the team should have used the unlocked state if they wanted the option to change it later
Immutability can only be disabled by a Global Administrator
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Locked immutability is irreversible: once a vault's immutability is locked, it cannot be turned off, which is the point — it guarantees backup data cannot be deleted or modified even by an administrator. The unlocked state allows changes; the locked state does not. B is wrong: the greyed-out option is the intended behaviour. D is wrong: no role can unlock it. A is wrong: there is no 180-day unlock timer.

questions.question: Contoso's backup vault has a soft delete retention of 180 days. A colleague says this means deleted backups are kept for 180 days and the vault costs nothing extra. What is the correct cost understanding?
options: Soft delete retention is free up to 180 days, then billed
Soft delete only bills for the first 14 days, regardless of the configured window
Soft-deleted backups cost nothing, because they are not counted as stored data
Soft-deleted backup items still consume storage and are billed during the retention window, because the data is retained for recovery; a longer window means more retained data and higher storage cost
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Soft-deleted items are retained data and consume storage during the retention window, so they are billed; extending the window to 180 days increases the retained data and the cost. C is wrong: retained data is stored data. A and D invent free periods that do not exist.

questions.question: Contoso wants to restore a single file from a VM backup without restoring the whole VM. A colleague says this is impossible and the whole VM must be restored. What is the correct capability?
options: File-level restore only works for Azure Files, never for VM backups
File-level restore requires cross-region restore
The whole VM must be restored, because file-level restore does not exist for VM backups
File-level (item-level) restore is supported for Azure VM backups: the team can restore individual files from a VM backup recovery point without restoring the entire VM
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Azure Backup supports file-level (item-level) restore from VM backup recovery points, so a single file can be recovered without restoring the whole VM. C is wrong: item-level restore exists. A is wrong: it exists for VM backups as well as Azure Files. B is wrong: item-level restore does not require CRR.

questions.question: Contoso's backup policy is configured with a daily backup and a retention of 30 days. A colleague says the 30-day retention means backups are kept for 30 days after the last backup, and then all recovery points vanish at once. What is the correct understanding?
options: All recovery points vanish at once on day 31
Retention is per recovery point: each daily recovery point is retained for 30 days from when it was created, so recovery points expire on a rolling basis, not all at once
Retention applies to the vault, not to recovery points, so nothing expires
Retention is 30 days from the first backup only, so after 30 days no recovery points remain
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Retention applies per recovery point: each backup's recovery point is kept for the retention period from its creation date, so points expire on a rolling basis as they age out. A is wrong: expiry is rolling, not simultaneous. C is wrong: retention does apply to recovery points. D is wrong: the window is per point, not from the first backup.

questions.question: Contoso wants to back up an Azure VM that has a large data disk, but the backup window is short. A colleague proposes excluding the data disk from backup. What should the team consider?
options: Disks cannot be excluded from Azure VM backup under any circumstances
Excluding a disk automatically enables cross-region restore for it
Excluding the data disk is always safe, because data disks are never needed in a restore

The team can exclude disks from a VM backup, but an excluded disk's data will not be recoverable from that backup; the decision must be based on whether the disk's data is protected elsewhere or is truly disposable
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Azure VM backup supports excluding disks, but the excluded disk is not protected by that backup; the team must ensure the data is protected elsewhere or is disposable before excluding it. C is wrong: excluding a disk that holds needed data loses that data on restore. A is wrong: disk exclusion is supported. B is wrong: exclusion and CRR are unrelated.

questions.question: Contoso's security team wants to ensure backup data is encrypted. A colleague says Azure Backup stores data unencrypted and the team must encrypt it themselves. What is the correct understanding?
options: Azure Backup encrypts data only if cross-region restore is enabled
Azure Backup encrypts data only for VMs, not for file shares or databases
Azure Backup stores data unencrypted, so the team must encrypt it before backup
Azure Backup encrypts data at rest (with Microsoft-managed keys by default, and customer-managed keys available) and in transit, so backup data is encrypted without the team encrypting it first
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Azure Backup encrypts backup data at rest (Microsoft-managed keys by default, with customer-managed keys as an option) and in transit; the team does not need to pre-encrypt. C is wrong: encryption is built in. A is wrong: encryption does not depend on CRR. B is wrong: encryption applies across backup workloads.
questions.source_title: Overview of security and cyber recovery in Azure Backup
questions.source_quote: "Soft delete delays permanent deletion and keeps deleted backup data recoverable during its configured retention period. The default retention period is 14 days and can be extended up to 180 days."

questions.question: Contoso wants to use customer-managed keys (CMK) for backup encryption, so that the organisation controls the encryption keys. A colleague says CMK is not supported for Azure Backup. What is the correct guidance?
options: CMK is not supported for Azure Backup, so the team must use Microsoft-managed keys
Customer-managed keys are supported for Azure Backup (via Azure Key Vault), letting the organisation control the keys used to encrypt backup data at rest
CMK is only supported for Sentinel, not for Backup
CMK requires the vault to use locally-redundant storage
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Azure Backup supports customer-managed keys through Azure Key Vault, so the organisation can control the encryption keys for backup data at rest. A is wrong: CMK is supported. C is wrong: CMK is a Backup encryption option, not a Sentinel-only feature. D is wrong: CMK does not depend on the storage redundancy type.
questions.source_title: Overview of security and cyber recovery in Azure Backup
questions.source_quote: "Soft delete delays permanent deletion and keeps deleted backup data recoverable during its configured retention period. The default retention period is 14 days and can be extended up to 180 days."

questions.question: Contoso's backup administrator leaves the company. The team discovers that the vault's Resource Guard is in a different subscription owned by the departed admin, and no one else can approve critical operations. What is the lesson, and what should the team have done?
options: Resource Guards should be deleted when an admin leaves, because they block all operations
MUA should never be used, because it creates this problem
Nothing can be done, because Resource Guards cannot be recovered

Resource Guards should be owned by a separate, durable security team (not a single individual), with multiple approvers, so that critical operations can still be approved when one person leaves; the team must re-establish ownership through the subscription owner
questions.explanation: Correct: D. A Resource Guard is a security boundary that must be owned durably: it should belong to a separate team or group with multiple approvers, not to a single individual, so that departures do not strand critical operations. The team must work with the subscription owner to re-establish control. C is wrong: ownership can be re-established through the subscription. A is wrong: deleting the guard removes the protection. B is wrong: MUA is the right control; the failure was in ownership, not in using MUA.
questions.source_title: Multiuser Authorization Using Resource Guard - Azure Backup
questions.source_quote: "A different user must own the Resource Guard instance. The backup admin must not have Contributor, Backup MUA Admin, or Backup MUA Operator permissions for Resource Guard in any scenario."

questions.question: Contoso wants to back up a VM and be able to restore it to a different Azure region for a disaster recovery test, without a regional outage. A colleague says cross-region restore only works during an actual outage. What is the correct understanding?
options: Cross-region restore requires the primary region to be deleted first
Cross-region restore only works during a declared regional outage
Cross-region restore can be used for a restore drill at any time (once CRR is enabled and data has replicated to the secondary region); it is not restricted to actual outages
Cross-region restore cannot be used for drills, only for real disasters
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Cross-region restore is a restore capability that can be exercised for drills once CRR is enabled and the backup data has replicated to the secondary region; it does not require an actual outage. B and D are wrong: there is no outage requirement. A is wrong: the primary region is not deleted to use CRR.
questions.source_title: Overview of security and cyber recovery in Azure Backup
questions.source_quote: "Soft delete delays permanent deletion and keeps deleted backup data recoverable during its configured retention period. The default retention period is 14 days and can be extended up to 180 days."

questions.question: Contoso manages Azure Policy as code: policies are stored in a Git repository and deployed through a pipeline. A colleague proposes editing policies directly in the portal for speed, and syncing back later. Why is this a bad idea?
options: Editing in the portal creates drift between the portal and the repository, so the next pipeline deployment overwrites the manual change (or the repository overwrites the portal); policy as code requires the repository to be the single source of truth, with changes reviewed in pull requests
Policy as code does not support pipelines, so portal edits are the only way
Portal edits are automatically synced to the repository, so there is no drift
Editing in the portal is the recommended approach, so the colleague is right
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Policy as code means the repository is the source of truth: manual portal edits create drift, and the next pipeline run will overwrite them (or the repo will be out of date). Changes should go through the repository with review. D is wrong: portal edits are the anti-pattern. B is wrong: policy as code is designed for pipelines. C is wrong: there is no automatic portal-to-repo sync.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso assigns a Deny policy that blocks the creation of public storage accounts. An Owner tries to create one and is blocked. A colleague says Owners can override Deny policies. What is the correct understanding?
options: A Deny policy effect blocks the non-compliant request even for Owners; no role, including Owner, can bypass a Deny assignment, which is why Deny is the strongest preventive control
Deny policies only block Readers, not Owners
Deny policies only apply to new subscriptions, not existing ones
Owners can override Deny policies, so the block must be a bug
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A Deny effect prevents the resource creation regardless of the caller's role; even an Owner cannot bypass a Deny assignment. D is wrong: Owners cannot override Deny. B is wrong: Deny applies to all roles. C is wrong: Deny applies to the assignment scope, not only new subscriptions.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso wants a policy that automatically adds a required tag to any resource group created without it. A colleague proposes a Deny policy. What is the correct policy effect, and what does it need?
options: A Deny policy, because Deny can add tags
An Audit policy, because Audit adds tags automatically

A Modify policy (or deployIfNotExists), which remediates non-compliant resources by adding the tag; it needs a managed identity with permission to write tags, because remediation runs as that identity
A Disabled policy, because Disabled enforces tagging
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Modify (and deployIfNotExists) effects remediate non-compliant resources — for example, adding a missing tag — and they run under a managed identity that needs permission to perform the remediation (such as writing tags). A is wrong: Deny blocks creation; it does not add tags. B is wrong: Audit only reports non-compliance. D is wrong: Disabled means the policy does not evaluate.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso creates a new Azure Policy assignment for a policy that audits VMs without Azure Monitor Agent. The team checks compliance immediately and sees no results. A colleague says the assignment failed. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The policy must be a Deny policy to produce results
The assignment failed, because compliance results are instant

Policy evaluation runs on resource creation/update, on assignment creation or update, and on a periodic cycle (about every 24 hours); compliance results appear after the next evaluation, not instantly
Audit policies never produce compliance results
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Azure Policy evaluates resources when they are created or updated, when an assignment is created or updated, and on a roughly 24-hour cycle; compliance data appears after evaluation, not immediately. B is wrong: the delay is normal. D is wrong: Audit policies do produce compliance results. A is wrong: the effect does not determine whether results appear.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso wants to test a new Deny policy before enforcing it, to see how many existing resources would be non-compliant. A colleague proposes assigning it as Deny immediately and watching for complaints. What is the safer approach?
options: Assign it first with the Audit effect (or in audit mode) to measure non-compliance without blocking anything, then switch to Deny once the impact is understood; Learn recommends starting with Audit
Assign it as Disabled, because Disabled measures non-compliance
There is no way to test a policy before enforcing it
Assign it as Deny immediately, because that is the only way to test a policy
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Learn recommends starting with the Audit effect to see what would be non-compliant without blocking deployments, then moving to Deny (or Enforce) once the impact is understood. D is wrong: immediate Deny risks breaking legitimate deployments. B is wrong: Disabled does not evaluate. C is wrong: Audit mode is the test mechanism.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso deploys infrastructure with Bicep. A colleague writes a Bicep file that creates a storage account with public blob access enabled, and the deployment succeeds. A colleague says Bicep prevents insecure configurations. What is the correct understanding?
options: Bicep automatically enables private endpoints for all storage accounts
Bicep files cannot create storage accounts, so the deployment must have used ARM directly
Bicep prevents insecure configurations, so the deployment should have failed

Bicep is a declarative language that deploys what is written; it does not by itself block insecure settings. Azure Policy (Deny) and secure defaults in the template are the controls that prevent public blob access
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Bicep deploys the resources as declared; it does not validate security posture. Preventing public blob access requires an Azure Policy Deny assignment and/or secure defaults in the template. C is wrong: Bicep has no built-in security blocking. A is wrong: Bicep does not auto-create private endpoints. B is wrong: Bicep can create storage accounts.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso stores a Bicep template in a repository. A colleague commits the template with a hardcoded storage account key in it, saying the repository is private so it is safe. What is the problem, and what should they do instead?
options: The problem is only that the key is a storage key; other secrets are fine in templates
The template should be deleted, because Bicep cannot reference Key Vault
There is no problem, because private repositories are safe for secrets

Hardcoded secrets in a template are a security risk even in a private repository (they spread through clones, logs and history); secrets should be referenced from Azure Key Vault (or passed as secure parameters) at deployment time, never committed in the template
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Secrets must never be committed in templates: they leak through clones, CI logs and git history. The correct pattern is to reference secrets from Azure Key Vault at deployment time (secure parameters / Key Vault references). C is wrong: private does not mean safe for secrets. A is wrong: all secrets are the problem, not just storage keys. B is wrong: Bicep can reference Key Vault.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso uses Deployment Stacks to manage a set of resources as one unit. A colleague deletes a resource from the stack's template and redeploys, expecting the resource to remain because it is still in use. What happens, and which setting controls it?
options: The resource remains, because Deployment Stacks never delete resources

The resource is deleted (or detached) depending on the stack's actionOnUnmanage setting: deleteAll/deleteResources removes unmanaged resources, while detachAll leaves them in place but unmanaged; the team must choose the setting deliberately
The deployment fails, because resources cannot be removed from a stack
The resource is automatically moved to another stack
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Deployment Stacks treat the template as the single cohesive unit: when a resource is removed from the template, the stack's actionOnUnmanage setting determines what happens to it — deleteAll/deleteResources removes the unmanaged resource, while detachAll leaves it in place but unmanaged. The team must choose the setting deliberately. A is wrong: stacks can delete unmanaged resources. C is wrong: the deployment does not fail when a resource is removed from the template. D is wrong: resources are not moved to another stack.
questions.source_title: Create and deploy Azure deployment stacks in Bicep
questions.source_quote: "An Azure deployment stack is a resource that enables you to manage a group of Azure resources as a single, cohesive unit."

questions.question: Contoso creates a Deployment Stack with deny settings that prevent changes outside the stack. A Contributor tries to modify a resource in the stack directly and is blocked. A colleague says Contributors can bypass deny settings. What is the correct understanding?
options: Deny settings on a Deployment Stack block changes by users who lack the required permission; a Contributor cannot create or delete deny assignments (only an Owner can), and cannot bypass the deny settings to modify the managed resources
Deny settings only block Readers, not Contributors
Deny settings only apply to new resources, not existing ones
Contributors can bypass deny settings, so the block must be a bug
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Deployment Stacks deny settings prevent out-of-band changes to managed resources; a Contributor cannot create or delete deny assignments (that requires Owner), and cannot bypass the deny settings. D is wrong: Contributors cannot bypass deny settings. B is wrong: deny settings apply to all roles without the required permission. C is wrong: they apply to the managed resources, existing and new.
questions.source_title: Create and deploy Azure deployment stacks in Bicep
questions.source_quote: "An Azure deployment stack is a resource that enables you to manage a group of Azure resources as a single, cohesive unit."

questions.question: Contoso manages its Azure environment with ARM templates and wants to move to a model where a set of resources is deployed and managed as a single lifecycle unit, with cleanup when the unit is retired. A colleague proposes Azure Blueprints. What is the current recommended approach?
options: Azure Blueprints, because it is the current recommended tool for lifecycle management

Deployment Stacks, which manage a set of resources as a single cohesive unit with lifecycle operations (deploy, update, delete) and deny settings; Blueprints is being retired and Microsoft directs customers to Deployment Stacks and Template Specs
Azure Policy, because it deploys resources as a unit
Sentinel playbooks, because they manage resource lifecycles
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Deployment Stacks are the current recommended way to manage a set of Azure resources as a single unit with a shared lifecycle; Azure Blueprints is being retired and Microsoft directs customers to Deployment Stacks and Template Specs. A is wrong: Blueprints is retired, not recommended. C is wrong: Policy governs compliance; it does not deploy resource sets. D is wrong: playbooks respond to Sentinel incidents.

questions.source_quote: "An Azure deployment stack is a resource that enables you to manage a group of Azure resources as a single, cohesive unit."

questions.question: Contoso wants to ensure that every new resource group in a subscription gets a standard set of policies (tagging, allowed locations, allowed SKUs) applied automatically. A colleague proposes creating the policies manually for each resource group. What is the correct mechanism?
options: A Sentinel analytics rule, because it applies policies
Create the policies manually for each resource group, because automation is impossible
An Azure Policy initiative (a collection of policy definitions) assigned at the subscription or management group scope, so the standard set applies to all current and future resource groups in scope
A Deployment Stack per resource group, because stacks apply policies
questions.explanation: Correct: C. A policy initiative groups multiple policy definitions (tagging, allowed locations, allowed SKUs) into one assignment at subscription or management group scope, so the standard applies to all current and future resource groups in scope. B is wrong: manual per-group creation is unscalable and error-prone. D is wrong: Deployment Stacks deploy resources; they do not assign policy initiatives. A is wrong: analytics rules detect threats; they do not assign policies.

questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso's pipeline deploys a Bicep template that creates a Key Vault. A colleague proposes setting the vault's access policies in the same template, and another says to use Azure RBAC for Key Vault instead. Which is the current recommended approach, and why?
options: Access policies, because RBAC is only for storage accounts
Access policies in the template, because RBAC cannot control Key Vault access

Azure RBAC for Key Vault (the Azure role-based access control permission model), which is the recommended way to control access to Key Vault data and management plane, replacing the legacy access policies model
Neither, because Key Vault access cannot be controlled in a template
questions.explanation: Correct: C. Azure RBAC is the recommended permission model for Key Vault: it controls access to keys, secrets and certificates through Azure roles, replacing the legacy access policies model. B is wrong: RBAC can control Key Vault access. D is wrong: Key Vault access is controllable in templates via RBAC role assignments. A is wrong: RBAC is not limited to storage accounts.

questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso wants to validate a Bicep template before deploying it, to catch errors such as a reference to a non-existent resource. A colleague says the only validation is to deploy it. What should they do instead?
options: Deploy it, because there is no pre-deployment validation for Bicep
Use the what-if deployment operation (and Bicep build / lint) to preview changes and catch errors before deploying, so mistakes are found without creating or modifying resources
Use a Sentinel hunting query to validate the template
Use the Secure Score to validate the template
questions.explanation: Correct: B. The what-if operation previews exactly which resources would be created, modified or deleted, and Bicep build/lint catches syntax and reference errors before deployment; deploying to validate is unnecessary and risky. A is wrong: pre-deployment validation exists. C is wrong: hunting queries search log data, not templates. D is wrong: the Secure Score measures cloud posture.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy
questions.source_quote: "Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules."

questions.question: Contoso's team is migrating from Azure Blueprints to Deployment Stacks. A colleague says Blueprints will keep working indefinitely, so the migration can wait. What is the correct timeline pressure, and what should the team do?
options: Azure Blueprints is being retired (Microsoft's published timeline: no new blueprint definitions from 31 July 2026, full retirement 31 January 2027), so the team should migrate its blueprints to Deployment Stacks and Template Specs before retirement
Blueprints was already retired in 2024, so the team must have been using something else
Blueprints is being replaced by Sentinel playbooks, so the team should migrate there
Blueprints will keep working indefinitely, so there is no urgency
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Azure Blueprints is being retired: Microsoft's published timeline stops new blueprint definitions from 31 July 2026 and retires the service on 31 January 2027, so the team should migrate to Deployment Stacks and Template Specs. (Sourcing note: the retirement dates come from Microsoft's published retirement timeline as reported in secondary sources; the migration targets — Deployment Stacks and Template Specs — are confirmed in the Deployment Stacks documentation.) D is wrong: retirement is scheduled. B is wrong: the retirement is in 2026–2027, not 2024. C is wrong: playbooks are a Sentinel SOAR mechanism, not a Blueprint replacement.
